episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 16, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education. At Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are struggling to validate online assessments in the age of A.I.

<break time="0.5s"/>

In Insights & Trends today, according to Denver7, faculty at Metropolitan State University Denver are facing significant challenges in student assessment, particularly with the rise of A.I. Jeff Loats, a professor and director at MSU's Center for Teaching, Learning and Design, expressed concerns over the validity of online assessments. He noted, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way." Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, views this as an opportunity to improve assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer has adjusted his journalism class format, moving from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person assignments. This shift encourages assignments that require students to apply knowledge to real-life scenarios, which are less easily completed by A.I. However, Schafer acknowledges the difficulty for instructors to drastically change their teaching methods. Faculty responses vary widely, with some allowing limited A.I. use and others restricting it entirely. The challenge of setting definitive guidelines across over 100 majors at MSU highlights the evolving nature of institutional responses.

<break time="0.75s"/>

Over at Universidad Austral, in our Case Study category, Times Higher Education reports a partnership with Universidad de La Sabana to develop an intelligent dashboard for student assessment. This tool allows educators and students to interact with A.I. as both a teammate and teaching assistant. It provides continuous feedback and helps students develop better judgment in A.I. use. Early results suggest the dashboard could enhance student learning by offering insights into their performance.

<break time="0.75s"/>

Meanwhile, in Practical Tips today, the San Diego Community College District is preparing for InnovAItion Day on March 20. According to City Times, the event will bring together faculty, staff, and students to explore responsible A.I. use in education. It will feature student-led panels and discussions that examine A.I.'s role in enhancing the learning experience. This initiative aims to foster a comprehensive understanding of A.I. among the academic community.

<break time="0.75s"/>

Turning to another Case Study, UNC Greensboro's School of Nursing is taking significant steps in A.I. integration. According to UNC Greensboro, the school has appointed A.I. Champions to incorporate artificial intelligence across curriculum, simulation, and faculty training. Seventy percent of faculty are actively using A.I. tools to enhance student engagement and support different learning styles. This approach highlights the school's commitment to modernizing nursing education.

<break time="0.75s"/>

And here's one worth watching. George Washington University is also adapting to the A.I. era. GW Today reports that Professor Michael Tadesse has restructured his marketing courses to focus on an "innovation mindset lab." In this lab, students collaborate with real businesses to create A.I.-enabled prototypes. This approach emphasizes strategic thinking and adaptability, moving beyond traditional content delivery to prepare students for the future business landscape.

<break time="0.75s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

topStory.headline: MSU Denver Faculty Say Online Assessments Have Become Impossible to Validate
topStory.summary:
At Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are confronting challenges with student assessment in the A.I. age, according to Denver7. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, stated that if assessments are online, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way."

Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, described this as an opportunity to "right the ship" on assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer described flipping his journalism class from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person assignments. He anticipates more case studies and "apply this to your life, apply to your community" assignments because these are harder for A.I. to complete authentically.

Schafer acknowledged that it is difficult for instructors to drastically change their teaching methods, and faculty buy-in varies. Some professors allow limited A.I. use while others restrict it entirely, creating a patchwork approach. The challenge of creating definitive guidelines across more than 100 majors at MSU illustrates how institutional responses are still evolving.
